title: This Tiny Blob Sets a New Record for Hottest Life on Earth
summary:
Imagine a creature that loves water so hot it would burn your hand. Scientists just found one! It's a tiny, single-celled blob called an amoeba. Its nickname is the 'fire amoeba from the Cascades.'

The amoeba was discovered in Lassen Volcanic National Park in California. It grows and splits in water that is 145 degrees Fahrenheit. That's hotter than a cup of coffee! Before this, no complex cell had ever been found living above 140 degrees.

Amoebas are not animals, plants, or fungi. They are just one cell, but they are more complex than bacteria. This new one, named Incendiamoeba cascadensis, was found in a hot stream. When it gets too hot — 158 degrees — it builds a little shell and goes to sleep. When things cool down, it wakes up again.

But it has a limit. At 176 degrees, it doesn't survive. The scientist who found it, Beryl Rappaport, said she was 'very surprised.' She even had to check her tools to make sure they were right!
why_it_matters: It shows that even the tiniest living things can survive in places that seem impossible, which makes you wonder what else is hiding in nature — maybe even in a park you could visit one day.

background_read: Lassen Volcanic National Park in California really does have hot springs and steaming ground, because a volcano sits under it.
Other super-tough tiny creatures, sometimes called 'extremophiles', live in boiling hot springs in places like Yellowstone National Park in the United States.
Scientists study these heat-loving creatures because they want to know whether life could survive in extreme places on other planets.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists, including Beryl Rappaport, who found a new single-celled amoeba.
WHAT: The amoeba can grow and split in water at 145 degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than any complex cell ever found before.
WHERE: In a hot stream in Lassen Volcanic National Park in California.
WHY: It shows life can survive in hotter places than anyone thought, so scientists have to rethink the limits of life.

perspectives.description: They think this is a big deal because it pushes the limit of where life can exist and gives them new questions to study.
They want other scientists to test the same hot water with their own tools before everyone agrees it is truly a record.
They say this shows how special hot springs are, and why we should protect strange places where unusual life can grow.
